description: Oman Mars is a team of curious minds passionate about space, science, and real-world problem solving. We believe Oman has a unique role to play in the future of space exploration, and we use NASA's open data to turn that belief into simple, practical tools for Earth and beyond.
summary: Oman Mars is an open, data-driven engine that suggests places on Earth that resemble Mars and could support future Moon and Mars base missions. Most projects only map a few famous analog sites. We split Oman into 85 grid cells (0.5°, about 50 km) and give each one a 0–100 score from open data. We use NASA Worldview/GIBS MODIS satellite imagery, 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA POWER climate data (temperature swing, humidity, rain, sunlight, wind, cloud) and SoilGrids soil data. The engine suggests the top 5 sites, and users can switch presets or change the weights with sliders. It has three modes: Mars-likeness, rocket launch and landing, and environmental sensitivity, which helps missions avoid fragile areas. A geology layer adds dunes, salt flats, ophiolite rocks and caves, and marks the real AMADEE-18 Mars simulation site. Nobody told the engine where Oman’s spaceport is, yet it ranked the Etlaq spaceport cell in Duqm 7th of 85. Choosing analog sites still depends mostly on expert judgment, and there is no widely used standard score. Our method is transparent, bilingual and reusable by any country as a first screening step before field visits.
details:
What it does
Oman Mars is a web-based suggestion engine that finds places on Earth that resemble Mars and places that suit rocket launch and landing. Teams preparing for Moon and Mars bases need both. We split Oman into 85 grid cells (0.5°, about 50 km) and give each cell a score from 0 to 100. The engine then suggests the top 5 sites, each at least 90 km apart.

How it works

  • Each cell gets 25-year averages (2001–2025) from NASA POWER: daily temperature swing, maximum temperature, humidity, rain, sunlight, wind at 2 m and 50 m, and cloud cover.
    1. Mars-likeness: climate and soil.
    2. Launch & landing: distance to the coast, latitude, calm winds, clear skies, flat and firm ground.
    3. Environmental sensitivity: distance to 6 nature reserves, rain, soil life and coastline, so missions can avoid fragile areas.
  • Clicking a cell opens a card. It shows the region, score, rank, coordinates and a chart comparing the cell with Mars values from NASA’s Curiosity rover (REMS, Gale Crater).
  • The map is live NASA Worldview/GIBS MODIS imagery. Black gaps between satellite passes are filled from earlier days.
  • A geology layer marks dunes, a salt flat, ophiolite rocks, a cave, and the real AMADEE-18 Mars simulation site (2018).

Validation
We never told the engine where Oman’s spaceport is, yet in launch mode it ranked the Etlaq spaceport cell in Duqm 7th of 85. Four cells stay in the top 10 under all four Mars presets, so the result is stable.

Benefits and impact
Choosing analog sites still depends mostly on expert judgment, and there is no widely used standard score. Our method is open, transparent and repeatable. It gives a fast first screening before costly field visits, and any country can reuse it. It can help analog-mission organisers, space agencies, spaceports, researchers and schools. It also supports Oman’s Space Policy 2023–2033. Our year-1 plan costs 4,650 OMR (hosting, development and field surveys) and starts with a 3-month pilot with one partner.

Tools

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single-page site.
  • Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map.
  • NASA GIBS WMTS tiles, the NASA POWER API and SoilGrids 2.0.
  • Playwright for automated testing on mobile and desktop.
  • Netlify for hosting.
  • Claude, an AI assistant, helped write and test the code.

Creativity
We built a ranking engine instead of a map of a few famous sites. The same engine answers three questions: is it like Mars, can you launch or land there, and is it environmentally sensitive. The site is bilingual (Arabic/English) and works on phones.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about limits: scores are relative within Oman, cells are 50 km wide, and SoilGrids is weaker in deserts.
  • Climate is not geology: AMADEE-18 ranks only around 60/85 in Mars mode because of sea humidity. That is why we added the geology layer.
  • Safety: a salt flat can look flat in the data but is unsafe for landing.
  • The environment.
  • Mobile users and Arabic-speaking users.
  • Openness: every data source is listed with links at https://subtle-dodol-5e6577.netlify.app/sources.html
